title: Liberalism needs a new philosophy of immigration
gist: The AfD's landslide in Saxony-Anhalt kills the thesis that the far-right surge was pandemic-era incumbent anger; Smith argues immigration is the driver, citing research that a 1% rise in immigration stocks lifts far-right voting 1.78-2.97%. He calls on liberals to replace tactical immigration pauses with three avowed principles — migration is not a human right, immigration law is legitimate and must be enforced, and immigration must benefit existing citizens — as the only sustainable way to defuse the global anti-immigration backlash.

themes.theme: AfD landslide kills the Covid-backlash thesis

insights.claim: Germany's AfD won a landslide in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, which does not mean it is taking over Germany — the far right is far more popular in the post-communist east than in the more populous west — but is a warning shot the whole of Europe is taking seriously.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Regional far-right breakthroughs precede national coalition math problems; watch German western-state polling for the real escalation signal.
insights.locator: So, Germany’s far-right party, the AfD

insights.claim: The 2024-25 pundit thesis that US and European voters were backing rightist leaders out of Covid-era anger at incumbents is now dead, because the far-right surge has continued and intensified well past the pandemic.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: If the populist right is structurally rather than cyclically driven, political risk in Europe does not mean-revert — price it as persistent.
insights.locator: First, it means that the rise of far-right parties

insights.claim: AfD's flaws are catastrophic and well known — obvious ties to Vladimir Putin, a party filled with crooks, extreme rhetoric, no governing experience — so the fact that voters now overlook them measures the intensity of the underlying grievance.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Voter tolerance for Kremlin-aligned parties is a direct European security risk channel; rising AfD share is a NATO-cohesion negative.
insights.locator: Second, it means that something is making many German voters so angry

insights.claim: Adam Tooze, who leans strongly left, concedes AfD voters cite security, foreigners, woke politics and remoteness first when asked why they voted AfD, with economic issues barely mentioned — voting AfD is a vote to crack down on foreigners, not to get social democracy.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A left-wing source conceding the immigration driver removes the main intellectual cover for the 'more welfare wins them back' strategy.
insights.quote: It is a vote to crackdown on foreigners
insights.locator: Adam Tooze, who strongly leans to the left

insights.claim: Robin Brooks attributes the AfD surge to the CDU-SPD grand coalition proving incapable of confronting immigration with the urgency voters want — an incumbent-competence failure, not an economic one.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Grand-coalition failure to deliver on immigration is the mechanism converting voter anger into far-right seat share — track German enforcement statistics, not rhetoric.
insights.quote: A key driver of the recent surge in AfD popularity is that the CDU - SPD grand coalition is proving itself incapable of confronting immigration with the urgency many voters want.
insights.locator: Robin Brooks is more blunt

themes.theme: Quantifying immigration's effect on far-right voting

insights.claim: Konstantinou and Roumanias (2024), using over 4,500 regional electoral outcomes in Western Europe between 2000 and 2017 and instrumenting domestic immigration with immigration in neighboring countries, find a 1% increase in immigration stocks raises far-right voting by between 1.78% and 2.97%.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A usable elasticity for forecasting European electoral risk from migration flows — roughly a 2-3x amplification into far-right vote share.
insights.quote: a 1% increase in immigration stocks leads to a between 1.78% and 2.97% in Far-Right voting
insights.locator: Here are Konstantinou and Roumanias (2024)

insights.claim: The instrumented estimates are positive, significant and larger than simple OLS and fixed-effects results, and explain a large part of the observed far-right rise in high-immigration Western European countries — meaning naive regressions understate the effect.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Causal identification matters: models built on OLS estimates systematically underestimate political risk from migration.
insights.quote: The estimated effects of immigration are positive, significant and larger compared to those obtained by simple OLS and fixed effects regressions.
insights.locator: We use regional data spanning over 4500 electoral outcomes

insights.claim: The trend long predates 2026: Brookings documented in 2024 that the European Parliament election, France's snap election, three German state elections and the Austrian election all showed rightward drift and forced mainstream parties toward securitized, hardline migration positions.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Mainstream-party convergence on restriction is already the base case across the EU — policy risk is one-directional.
insights.locator: 2026 is hardly the beginning of the trend

insights.claim: Trump's 2024 election was partially about immigration: Trump voters rated it a top issue alongside inflation, and it was where Trump held his strongest polling lead over Kamala Harris, with American voters clearly souring on immigration in 2023-24.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Immigration was a decisive US electoral variable, implying continued restrictionist pressure on labor supply through the cycle.
insights.locator: Trump’s election in 2024 was also partially about immigration

themes.theme: The global restriction wave is already underway

insights.claim: Germany's CDU has already stanched migration flows with restrictive policies and Chancellor Friedrich Merz is responding to AfD gains by making citizenship harder to obtain, while France and Italy tighten border controls, France tightens citizenship, the EU toughens asylum rules, and Sweden pays migrants large sums to leave.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A synchronized OECD-wide immigration tightening is a structural negative for European labor force growth and a tailwind to wage pressure.
insights.quote: Sweden is offering migrants large sums of money to leave the country.
insights.locator: Germany’s center-right CDU has already stanched the flow

insights.claim: Even Canada — one of the most immigration-friendly and progressive countries on Earth, under Mark Carney's center-left government — has cut permanent resident targets, reduced student visas and slashed temporary worker numbers, with immigration levels still high but falling quickly.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Canadian population growth is decelerating sharply under a center-left government — directly relevant to Canadian housing demand, rents and GDP-per-capita math.
insights.locator: Even Canada, one of the most immigration-friendly

insights.claim: Japan is tightening its own immigration policies after a period of liberalization, showing the restriction wave is not confined to Europe and North America.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Japanese labor supply tightening compounds an already severe demographic squeeze — supports structural wage and automation investment themes there.
insights.locator: Japan is tightening its own immigration policies

insights.claim: Voters will likely read current restrictive measures as superficial tactical pauses designed to let populist anger simmer before permissive policies resume — exactly what happened in Europe, which halted Middle Eastern asylum admissions in the late 2010s after outcry and then resumed en masse in the 2020s.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Policy credibility, not policy level, determines whether the far-right vote share recedes — watch for explicit doctrinal commitments, not just enforcement numbers.
insights.quote: tactical pauses to let populist anger simmer down before resuming the same permissive immigration policies that made voters mad in the first place
insights.locator: And yet I’m worried that voters around the world

insights.claim: Biden mostly closed the border to asylum-seekers in 2024 once he saw the political damage, yet many Democrats now call for abolishing ICE — the same credibility-destroying oscillation playing out in the US.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Democratic immigration positioning is the key uncertainty for post-Trump US labor supply policy; ICE abolition rhetoric is a credibility liability.
insights.locator: And it also seems to be true in the U.S.

insights.claim: If Democrats actually abolish federal immigration enforcement rather than reshuffling and renaming agencies, Americans will realize within a couple of years that the difference between 'open borders' and 'immigration laws with no one to enforce them' is largely semantic.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A specific falsifiable political forecast: anti-ICE positioning is popular now but carries a ~2-year backlash fuse.
insights.quote: the difference between “open borders” and “immigration laws with no one to enforce them” is largely semantic
insights.locator: But if Democrats actually try to abolish federal immigration enforcement

insights.claim: Anti-immigration sentiment in the US is cyclical and reflexive: it spiked in 2023-24 in response to Biden's permissive asylum policies and crashed again once Trump took power and began committing abuses — and it will keep rising again and again unless liberals change their underlying approach.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Current pro-immigration polling is a Trump-backlash artifact, not a durable shift — do not extrapolate it into post-Trump policy assumptions.
insights.locator: We saw this in the U.S. in 2023-24

themes.theme: Three principles for a sustainable liberal immigration policy

insights.claim: Liberals must first admit that migration is not a human right: in a world of sovereign nation-states, nations are necessarily exclusive clubs with the right to restrict immigration for any reason, and borders are a fundamental part of the social compact that lets liberal nations exist at all.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The intellectual reframe center-left parties would need to adopt to neutralize the far right — a marker to watch in Democratic and European social-democratic platforms.
insights.quote: Liberals must therefore not view borders and citizenship as annoying obstacles to be tactically circumvented or overcome
insights.locator: The first thing liberals

insights.claim: The second principle is that immigration law is legitimate and must be enforced — treating undocumented status as a protected marginalized identity is absurd, comparable to treating drivers who speed as a minority group, because a law without enforcement is no law at all.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Defines the enforcement floor any durable liberal policy must accept; incompatible with ICE-abolition platforms.
insights.quote: it’s like if progressives decided that people who drive over the speed limit are a minority group
insights.locator: That means we need to recognize that immigration law is legitimate

insights.claim: The third principle is that immigration's purpose is to benefit the people already living in the receiving country — liberals must flatly reject Suketu Mehta's 'This Land is Our Land' framing of immigration as reparations for colonialism, a sacrifice Western nations owe others at their own expense.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A direct attack on the reparations framing that has gained purchase in progressive circles — a fault line to watch inside center-left coalitions.
insights.quote: We must flatly reject any concept of immigration that sees it as a necessary sacrifice on the part of American citizens.
insights.locator: A third principle that liberals should embrace

insights.claim: A liberal immigration program built on these three principles could permanently defuse anti-immigration sentiment across the developed world, but only if liberal leaders explicitly articulate and avow them — because the point is convincing voters the stand is principled rather than a retreat masking a hidden open-borders agenda.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The binding constraint is rhetorical credibility, not policy substance — expect the far-right vote share to persist until center parties make the explicit doctrinal turn.
insights.quote: that embracing the kind of immigration policies Americans demand represents a principled stand rather than a tactical retreat from a hidden agenda of open borders.
insights.locator: A liberal immigration program based on these three principles

themes.theme: Selectivity, economics, and the American frontier case

insights.claim: Skilled immigration brings far more economic benefit per capita and is more politically palatable, so a liberal system should explicitly tilt toward it — which American voters of both parties already want.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Points to a bipartisan landing zone: high-skilled visa expansion paired with restriction elsewhere — relevant to tech labor supply and H-1B-style policy bets.
insights.quote: Skilled immigrants bring far more economic benefits per capita than others
insights.locator: And if this requires us to be selective

insights.claim: Smith proposes barring immigrants who have belonged to groups that see America as evil, explicitly invoking the legal machinery once used to ban immigration by members of communist parties.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: An ideological-screening mechanism from an avowed pro-immigration liberal signals how far the Overton window has shifted on vetting.
insights.quote: let us bar immigrants who have been part of groups that see America as evil, using the law with which we once banned immigration by members of communist parties
insights.locator: Immigrants who don’t love and embrace American culture

insights.claim: The economic case for US immigration rests on higher tax revenue to shore up dangerously depleted government finances plus dominance in high-tech industries and innovation, while the real costs are narrow — local housing shortages and strains on local government finances — and the bulk of evidence finds immigrants do not reduce native wages or job opportunities.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Separates the two real cost channels (local housing, municipal finance) from the discredited wage-depression claim — the right place to target mitigation policy.
insights.quote: the bulk of the evidence concludes that immigrants don’t reduce wages or job opportunities for native-born Americans
insights.locator: Despite those reservations, I’ve always thought

insights.claim: American public opinion is not as restrictionist as online right-wing energy suggests: Gallup finds most Americans say immigration is good, and YouGov finds a fairly even split on whether the annual rate should be increased, decreased or kept the same.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The restrictionist online consensus overstates actual median-voter preference — a reason to expect policy to settle well short of maximal restriction.
insights.quote: rightists will direct online vitriol toward anyone who supports any immigration at all, but their energy and savagery shouldn’t be mistaken for majority support
insights.locator: And importantly, lots of Americans share my overall positive view

insights.claim: The proposed agenda would not be a far-right policy despite progressive labeling — it would still admit far more immigration than the policies of Franklin D. Roosevelt or Harry Truman.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A historical benchmark that reframes 'restriction' — useful for calibrating how much actual flow reduction current political pressure implies.
insights.quote: it would allow in far more immigration than the policies of Franklin D. Roosevelt or Harry Truman
insights.locator: For America, the kind of immigration agenda I’ve sketched out

insights.claim: Immigration policy is inherently a sovereign national decision, so JD Vance's attempt to tie America's immigration policy to France's or Germany's conflates fundamentally separate choices and should be rejected.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A framing fight over whether Western immigration politics is one transnational struggle or many national ones — shapes how contagious European far-right gains are to US politics.
insights.quote: JD Vance wants us to think that France’s immigration policy, or Germany’s, is inextricably tied to America’s. But it’s not
insights.locator: Because immigration is fundamentally the decision of each sovereign nation-state

insights.claim: Smith remains agnostic on other countries' immigration levels on Westphalian grounds — if a people decide immigration is unacceptably diluting their local culture they have every right to cut it off — while hoping they avoid being taken over by parties that take marching orders from the Kremlin.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Frames the real European downside risk as Russian-aligned capture rather than migration levels per se — an EU security and asset-risk consideration.
insights.quote: I hope they do what they need to do in order to avoid getting taken over by parties that take their marching orders from the Kremlin
insights.locator: As for the rest of the world
